module.title: SQL for Product Managers
module.subtitle: 50+ EXERCISES / 6 HOURS OF PRACTICE
module.description: Make decisions from data, not intuition. Query a real database with SQL in an embedded console. Case: a meditation app (Calmly).

lesson.title: SQL Essentials: Ask the Database
lesson.dataset: calmly (see data/calmly.schema.sql). Seed so the answer keys below hold.
lesson.note: All tasks use the embedded DuckDB-WASM SQL console. verdict/weight/feedback as in the base engine. Where a numeric answer is required, the console lets the learner derive it; grading is on the chosen option (optionally auto-verify the query result — see engine spec).

blocks.markdown: Welcome to the data team! Our product is **Calmly**, a meditation app. Everything users do lands in a Postgres database. As a PM you'll answer your own data questions instead of waiting in the analyst queue. Let's start simple.
This is our main table, `users`. Take a look at the schema on the left and run `SELECT * FROM users LIMIT 100`. How many **columns** does the `users` table have?
Right — 11 columns. Reading a schema is the first SQL skill: you can't query fields you don't know exist.
How many users signed up in **January 2024**? Filter `created_at` to that month and `COUNT` them.

config.defaultQuery:
SELECT COUNT(*) FROM users
WHERE created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND created_at < '2024-02-01'

blocks.markdown: 1,204. Note the boundary: use `< '2024-02-01'`, not `<= `, or you accidentally include Feb 1st. Half-open ranges are the safe habit for dates.
Hey, Growth PM here. Which **acquisition channel** brought the most users? Give me the top channel by count. (`GROUP BY channel`, `ORDER BY` count, `LIMIT 1`.)

config.defaultQuery:
SELECT channel, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM users
GROUP BY channel
ORDER BY n DESC

blocks.markdown: `organic` leads. `GROUP BY` + `ORDER BY count DESC` is the workhorse pattern for 'which category is biggest?' questions.
What's our **paid-subscription conversion rate** overall? That's premium users divided by all users, as a percent. Careful with integer division.

config.defaultQuery:
SELECT 100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN is_premium THEN 1 ELSE 0 END) / COUNT(*) AS conv_pct
FROM users

blocks.markdown: ~6.2%. If you got 0, you hit **integer division** — `premium/total` with integers truncates to 0. Multiply by `100.0` (a float) first, as in the query.
Marketing thinks paid channels bring premium users. Show the **premium conversion rate by channel**, highest first. Which channel converts best to premium?

config.defaultQuery:
SELECT channel,
  100.0 * SUM(CASE WHEN is_premium THEN 1 ELSE 0 END)/COUNT(*) AS conv_pct,
  COUNT(*) AS n
FROM users GROUP BY channel ORDER BY conv_pct DESC

options.label: referral — highest conversion, and a healthy user count
a tiny channel with 12 users and 50% conversion
organic — it has the most users

blocks.markdown: `referral` converts best with enough volume to trust. Watch for small-sample traps: a channel with 12 users at 50% isn't a real signal. Always look at the count alongside the rate.

Now a join. `sessions` logs every meditation session (one row per session, with `user_id`). What's the **average number of sessions per user** in January 2024? Think about which users count in the denominator.

config.defaultQuery:
SELECT COUNT(*) * 1.0 / COUNT(DISTINCT user_id) AS avg_sessions_per_user
FROM sessions
WHERE started_at >= '2024-01-01' AND started_at < '2024-02-01'

options.label: Impossible without a JOIN to users

blocks.markdown: ~4.7 per **active** user (`COUNT(DISTINCT user_id)` in the denominator). Dividing by all signups answers a different question (engagement across the whole base). Define your denominator on purpose.
I want the **7-day retention** for the January signup cohort: of users who signed up Jan 1–31, what % had at least one session 7+ days after signup? This needs a JOIN between `users` and `sessions`.

config.defaultQuery:
SELECT 100.0 * COUNT(DISTINCT s.user_id) / COUNT(DISTINCT u.id) AS d7_retention
FROM users u
LEFT JOIN sessions s
  ON s.user_id = u.id
  AND s.started_at >= u.created_at + INTERVAL '7 days'
WHERE u.created_at >= '2024-01-01' AND u.created_at < '2024-02-01'

blocks.markdown: ~28%. The JOIN condition carries the '7+ days after signup' logic; the `LEFT JOIN` keeps users with no qualifying session so the denominator stays the full cohort. Retention questions are cohort + time-offset joins.

A trap question. Someone reports 'average session length is 21 minutes' from `SELECT AVG(duration_min) FROM sessions`. You glance at the data and see a few sessions with `duration_min = 100000` (a logging bug). What should you do before trusting that average?

options.label: Use the MEDIAN, and/or filter outliers — the mean is distorted by bad rows
Report 21 minutes — AVG is the standard
Delete the whole sessions table and start over

blocks.markdown: Outliers wreck the mean. Check the distribution (`MIN`/`MAX`/percentiles), filter obvious bad rows, and prefer the **median** (`PERCENTILE_CONT(0.5)`) for skewed data. 'Communicating with data' includes sanity-checking it.
Final one. I need **new premium subscriptions per week** for a trend chart. Which query shape gives me a weekly time series?

config.defaultQuery:
SELECT date_trunc('week', premium_started_at) AS wk, COUNT(*) AS n
FROM users
WHERE is_premium
GROUP BY 1 ORDER BY 1

options.label: Just COUNT(*) with no GROUP BY

blocks.markdown: Bucket the timestamp with `date_trunc('week', ...)` then group by the bucket. Grouping by the raw timestamp gives one row per second — useless for a trend. This pattern powers almost every dashboard chart.

Nicely done. You can now read a schema, filter dates safely, group and rank, avoid integer-division and small-sample traps, join tables for retention, and bucket time for trends. That's most of a PM's daily SQL. Keep practicing on the full module.
